First-person view of a plague doctor who has just stepped into a poor peasant house in a small Northern European town during the plague of the 1630s, late at night. Only the doctor's black leather glove holding a long wooden cane is visible, entering the frame from the lower right corner.
The house is a single cramped room: a low ceiling with soot-blackened beams, cracked plaster walls, a beaten-earth floor with scattered straw, a hearth with dying embers on the left, a narrow wooden staircase on the right climbing into total darkness, and a box-bed built into the back wall with its heavy wool curtain drawn shut.
A family of three stands in the middle of the room, facing the doctor in tense silence, lit by a single tallow candle on a rough wooden table: a gaunt father in his forties with stubble and wary bloodshot eyes, standing protectively in front; a frightened mother in a linen coif, twisting her apron in her hands; a thin boy of about eight half-hidden behind her skirt, staring. They are hiding someone, and their faces show it.
On the table: a loaf of dark bread, a clay jug and four wooden bowls, although only three people are visible.
STYLE: an unsettling found photograph. Shot at night on old high-ISO film through a cheap lens: heavy grain, slight motion blur, crushed blacks, faded and desaturated colors with a sickly yellow-green cast, soft halation around the candle flame, dust specks and a faint light leak. It must look like a real photograph of real people, not a painting and not CGI: unidealized faces with pores, scars, uneven teeth and dirty skin, no beauty retouching.
Cinematic 16:9 composition. Everything outside the candlelight sinks into darkness. No text, no watermark, no frame or border.
